Robot Doctor Power & wiring

Robot loses power or reboots when things run

Everything cuts out for a second, the hub restarts, or motors stutter. Below are the 5 most common causes on FTC robots, ordered from most to least likely, with how to check and fix each one.

Skip the guesswork — run the interactive diagnosisAbout 6 quick questions narrow this list down to your robot's actual problem.

Quick checks first

  • Does it happen mostly when a big mechanism runs (flywheel, slides, intake) or when you push into something? Try driving around with nothing else running, then run the mechanism by itself.
  • Does it happen when the robot gets hit or jolted? Push the robot or tap the frame with your hand while it is running and see if it cuts out.
  • If you wiggle the battery and power cables while it's on, does the hub light flicker or the robot cut out? Gently wiggle the battery plug, the switch wires, and each XT30 at the hub one at a time.
  • Does the Driver Station show the voltage dropping to about 9 V or less when it happens? The battery voltage is at the top of the Driver Station screen. Watch it while you drive hard or run the mechanism.
  • Does it still happen with a freshly charged battery? Swap to a battery straight off the charger and repeat the exact same thing.
  • Does it happen right after touching a field wall, field element, or another robot? Think about the last few times. Was the robot touching something metal just before?
  • Does the motor hum or get hot without moving? Listen and carefully feel the motor after trying to run it.

Common causes and how to fix them

1 Too much current draw (brownout)

Flywheels, many servos, or stalled motors pull the battery voltage down until the control system resets or disconnects.

How to fix it 15 min

  1. Check whether the problem only happens when a specific mechanism runs. REV lists a disconnect sound, ≤9 V on the DS while running, and motors slower than commanded as brownout signs.
  2. Look for stalled motors: a jammed intake, a slide pushing a hard stop, or an arm held against gravity at full power. Stalls draw huge current.
  3. Stagger big loads in code (spin the flywheel up before you drive hard, not at the same time).
  4. Spread servos across hubs and use a Servo Hub or servo power injector for heavy ones.
  5. Keep the total under the 20 A battery fuse. Flywheels, LEDs, servo injectors, and cameras all add up.
Show battery voltage in telemetry
VoltageSensor battery = hardwareMap.voltageSensor.iterator().next();
// in your loop:
telemetry.addData("Battery (V)", "%.2f", battery.getVoltage());

Sources: REV · Control Hub troubleshooting · FTC Docs · Power management · FTC Docs · Servo power best practices

2 Loose power connection (XT30 / battery plug)

Compressed XT30 pins or a wiggly battery plug cut power for a split second when the robot gets bumped.

How to fix it 10 min

  1. With the robot on, wiggle the battery cable and each XT30 plug. If the hub light flickers or the DS beeps, you found it.
  2. Look at the male XT30 pins on the hub. Each pin has 4 tines with small gaps; if they are squeezed together, very gently spread them with an X-ACTO blade (REV's fix).
  3. Do not hot glue XT30 plugs. It only hides a bad contact, and the power still drops under impact.
  4. Strap the battery down so it cannot shift, and keep the cable away from sharp screws.
  5. Many teams swap the battery and switch leads to Anderson PowerPole connectors, which wear much better.

Sources: REV · Control Hub troubleshooting · FTC Docs · Annual maintenance · GM0 · Power tips and tricks

3 Battery is low or worn out

A tired battery sags under load, so motors slow down and the hub can brown out.

How to fix it 2 min

  1. Swap in a freshly charged battery and test again. That alone answers the question.
  2. Watch the voltage on the Driver Station while you drive hard. Healthy packs dip, but sitting around 9 V or lower under load is a problem.
  3. Charge at the rate the battery maker recommends (REV slim: 1.8 A on the REV charger; TETRIX: 0.9 A).
  4. Label every battery with your team number, the year, and a name, and tally charge cycles. NiMH packs get weak after roughly 200–300 cycles.
  5. Retire packs that drop fast even when full. A battery tester (like a Battery Beak) shows internal resistance.

Sources: FTC Docs · Battery care, charging, fuses · REV · Control Hub troubleshooting · REV · 12V battery troubleshooting

4 Static shock (ESD) from the field

Robots build static driving on tiles. When the frame touches metal, the discharge can reset the hub, the IMU, the camera, or Wi-Fi.

How to fix it 30 min

  1. Notice whether it happens right after touching a field element or another robot. That pattern is classic ESD.
  2. Install a FIRST-legal resistive grounding strap (REV-31-1269) from a spare XT30 port to the frame.
  3. Plug cameras and other USB devices into the Control Hub's USB 3.0 port. The USB 2.0 port has a known ESD issue that can knock out Wi-Fi.
  4. Mount electronics on a non-conductive panel (thin plywood, PVC) and keep exposed connector metal more than 3/8" (1 cm) from the frame. Arcs can jump that far.
  5. Snap ferrite chokes onto sensor, encoder, servo, and USB cables, and tape over exposed metal on servo extensions.
  6. Things touching the floor (foam wheels, a dragging intake) build static faster. Many teams wipe the robot with a dryer sheet between matches.

Sources: FTC Docs · Managing ESD · REV · General troubleshooting · GM0 · Wiring guide

5 Mechanism is jammed or overloaded

If the mechanism binds or the load is too heavy for the gearing, the motor stalls. It hums, heats up, and drains the battery.

How to fix it 15 min

  1. Power off and move the mechanism by hand through its full range. It should move smoothly with no tight spots.
  2. Feel the motor after a run. Hot means it is stalling or working far too hard.
  3. Check for over-tightened chain or belt, misaligned shafts, screws hitting things, or a hard stop the code keeps pushing into.
  4. If the load really is too heavy, add reduction or a second motor. The RoboCodex gear ratio calculator helps size it.

Sources: GM0 · Building tips · FTC Docs · Power management
